abstract: Microtubules are self-assembled biological hollow nanotubes composed by protein tubulin. They are essential for many biological functions, including cell motility, cell division, and act as intracellular track for organelle transport. In turn, through dynamic assembly and disassembly, they form spindle fibers for chromosome segregation during mitosis and meiosis. In this paper, we have measured the Raman spectra of microtubules and their constituent protein tubulin in dry powder form for a range of temperatures, from nitrogen liquid T=77 K up to room and physiological temperature T=310 K, to determine if molecular bond vibrations present potential Fano resonance asymmetry. We have found nontrivial persistence of Fano resonances, q<5, at room and physiological temperatures for some specific vibrational modes.

abstract: We have studied the impact of human amniotic membrane (hAM-pe) on wound closing speed in a scratch assay of human keratinocytes (HaCaT). Though not without limitations, scratch assays are useful for studying collective cellular displacement as a model of wound healing. We show that the treatment is effective in decreasing the average time that the cells need to completely close the wound, in agreement with previous \emph{in vivo} experiments. We developed an automated segmentation software, and verified that a linear fit, though not completely describing the wound edge dynamics, is a robust method for comparing treatments and control measurements. By tracking the individual motion of a subset of cells, we found that individual treatment does not cause an increase in individual speed enough to explain the effect of the treatment at the collective (wound edge) level. Instead, the mean squared displacement and numerical simulations of a simple model of interacting active Brownian particles support the view that the main effect of the treatment at the individual level is to increase the persistence of cellular motion.

abstract: PKD2 (TRPP1) is a TRPP ion channel whose dysfunction causes autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). Understanding its conformational states and gating mechanism is important for elucidating its function and for structure-based drug discovery. Cryo-EM structures of WT-PKD2 contain a local {pi}-helical turn in the S6 pore-lining helix ({pi}-conformation). In contrast, a fully -helical S6 (-conformation) was observed in the gain-of-function mutant F604P-PKD2 and interpreted as the open state, leading to the proposed {pi}-to- activation mechanism. However, whether the -conformation can support function has never been directly established. Here, using molecular dynamics simulations, we investigate the functional properties of the -and {pi}-conformations of PKD2. The -conformation remains dewetted unless the lower gate is widened beyond the conformational range observed in mammalian TRP channels. By contrast, the {pi}-conformation supports pore hydration and ion conduction following a small opening of the L677 gate, with simulated conductance comparable to experimental measurements. The closely related PKD2L1 (TRPP2) channel shows a similar dependence on conformation, with a hydrated {pi}-conformation and a dewetted -conformation. Together, these findings challenge the assignment of the -conformation as the conductive state and support a model in which the {pi}-conformation represents the functionally relevant state of TRPP channels. This model suggests that activation may involve an -to-{pi} transition rather than the previously proposed {pi}-to- transition, providing a new framework for understanding TRPP channel gating. This work sheds light on the molecular basis of polycystin channel dysfunction and could facilitate the development of PKD2-targeted therapeutic strategies for ADPKD.

title: TRPP Ion Channels Function in the π-Conformation Rather Than the α-Conformation

abstract: Protein-protein interactions (PPIs) regulate essential cellular processes, yet the evolutionary principles that shape their specificity, adaptability, and dysregulation in disease remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the evolution of a signaling PPI between the small GTPase Ras and its effector Nore1A, a tumor suppressor involved in Ras-mediated signaling. Ras acts as a molecular switch, engaging effectors in its GTP-bound active state and releasing them after GTP hydrolysis, whereas oncogenic mutations such as G12D lock Ras in the active state, promoting aberrant signaling in cancer. Using yeast surface display, deep mutational scanning, and data normalization, we systematically mapped the Ras/Nore1A binding landscape under different physiological and oncogenic states. We generated and screened $\sim$33,000 Nore1A single and double mutants against RasWT and RasG12D in both GTP- and GDP-bound states. Our data revealed that most Nore1A mutations produce small-to-moderate decrease in Ras affinity, while a small number of substitutions enhance affinity. Unexpectedly, GTP hydrolysis causes minimal remodeling of the interaction landscape. Conversely, the oncogenic RasG12D mutation reshapes the binding landscape, revealing many Nore1A variants with enhanced and selective affinity for mutant Ras. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of Nore1A-Ras variant complexes suggest that the non-optimality of the Nore1A/RasG12D binding landscape arises, in part, from the greater intrinsic flexibility of RasG12D and the pronounced reduction in flexibility induced by affinity-enhancing Nore1A mutations. These findings demonstrate that disease-associated mutations can create new evolutionary trajectories in signaling PPIs by changing interaction dynamics and provide a framework for engineering selective protein-based inhibitors targeting oncogenic Ras variants.
authors: Tomazini, A.; Gurusinghe, S.; Bogomolov, S.; Shifman, J. M.
title: The binding landscape of Ras/effector interactions provides insights on Ras switching and oncogenesis

abstract: The RNA-binding protein Hfq and inorganic polyphosphate (polyP) were previously suggested to promote DNA compaction of AT-rich regions by forming heterochromatin-like structures, yet the underlying molecular mechanism remains unclear. Here, we combine coarse-grained and all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the interplay between Hfq, polyP, and DNA. Under physiological conditions, polyP electrostatically interacts with the distal faces of multiple Hfq hexamers, clustering them near DNA and leaving the proximal faces available to interact with the DNA minor groove via the disordered N-termini, thereby promoting compaction.

title: Polyphosphate and Disordered Hfq Regions Drive DNA Compaction through Conformation-Dependent Interactions

abstract: Human cerebral arteries become increasingly, sometimes abnormally, winding with age, but the mechanical basis of this change remains incompletely understood. To examine how arterial bends form and what sets their spacing, we modeled a cerebral artery as a slender elastic vessel supported by surrounding tissue. The distance between its ends remains constant, and the vessel can bend only in a plane tangent to the brain surface. As its natural length increases, axial compression builds until the vessel buckles. Bending partly relieves the compression, and the resulting waves grow in amplitude as elongation continues. Arterial bending stiffness and tissue support determine the wavelength, which is much larger than and proportional to vessel diameter, with comparatively weak dependence on other parameters. Numerical simulations captured a pre-buckling phase, rapid amplification of waves, and slow post-buckling growth during continued elongation. We evaluated these predictions using three-dimensional centerlines of cerebral arteries reconstructed from magnetic resonance angiography in healthy adults. Older age was associated with greater arterial length and excess-length ratio. For arterial waves oriented mostly parallel to the brain surface, wavelength increased with vessel diameter. Both this relationship and the observed wavelength-to-diameter ratio were consistent with model predictions. However, wave amplitude was not significantly associated with age. Overall, the modeling and imaging results support growth-driven buckling and post-buckling deformation under spatial constraint as a plausible mechanical explanation for age-related cerebral arterial tortuosity. This framework links vascular aging to growth-driven instability and pattern formation, with potential applications to diseased arteries beyond the brain.

title: Growth-driven mechanical buckling as a mechanism of age-related tortuosity in human cerebral arteries

abstract: hnRNPA2 is a component of cellular membraneless organelles many of which contain RNA and RNA-binding proteins (RBPs). RBPs frequently contain low-complexity domains (LCDs) that can also assemble into amyloid fibrils. Fibrils isolated from patients with frontotemporal lobar degeneration contain ordered segments of these LCDs and disease-associated mutations can enhance the homotypic interactions that promote aggregation. Although previous studies have largely examined the condensate-to-fibril transition by altering condensate stability, how amyloid structure governs this process remains poorly understood. Here, we show that the hnRNPA2 LCD forms a reproducible fibril fold and by combining structure-guided thermodynamic profiling, peptide design, mutagenesis and in vitro characterization under conditions with (two-phase) and without (one-phase) condensates, we define the molecular determinants of its assembly. We identify an aromatic triad within the fibril core that controls fibril formation kinetics and thermodynamic stability. Mutational analysis further reveals that condensate stability and fibril stability are largely independent. Finally, microrheology linked reduced condensate viscosity to faster fibril formation, supporting a role for condensate material properties in regulating aggregation kinetics. Together, these findings support a model in which the condensate-to-fibril transition is governed by the interplay between a disordered ''fuzzy coat'' and a fibril-forming aromatic triad within hnRNPA2. This work provides a structural framework for understanding how condensates can transition into amyloid assemblies.
authors: Kieffer, D. J.; Hwang, J. H.; Rosen, M. K.; Joachimiak, L. A.
title: Amyloid stability and condensate material properties independently govern the hnRNPA2 condensate to fibril transition

abstract: The aggregation of -synuclein into amyloid fibrils is a hallmark of a collection of neurodegenerative diseases termed synucleinopathies, including Parkinson's disease (PD). Interactions between -synuclein and lipid membranes modulate -synuclein aggregation and can produce protofibril structures consisting of both protein and lipid, termed lipidic fibrils. These lipidic fibrils can mature into mature fibrils, which resemble ex vivo fibrils extracted from Lewy bodies found in post-mortem brain samples of PD patients. Here, through the combination of experiments and kinetic theory, we study the influence of lipids and lipidic fibrils on the formation of mature fibrils. We find that lipidic fibrils catalyze mature fibril formation via a heterogeneous primary nucleation mechanism, which lowers the activation energy barrier of mature fibril formation relative to lipid-independent primary nucleation. The final stage of the reaction is governed by mature fibril elongation becoming limited by the rate at which protein monomers dissociate from the metastable lipidic fibrils, confirming that fibrils form in order of stability following Ostwald's Rule of Stages. This mechanism is validated using the small molecule inhibitor ambroxol, which selectively suppresses the formation of lipidic fibrils and in this manner shifts the aggregation kinetics to the slow, lipid-independent pathway. Taken together, these findings reveal that lipidic fibrils act as on-pathway intermediates and accelerate the aggregation of mature fibrils, which could provide a quantitative framework to design novel therapeutic strategies to inhibit pathological -synuclein aggregation.
authors: Stevenson, A.; Dreier, J. E.; Baumgartner, N.; Christiansen, N. T.; Galvagnion, C.; Michaels, T. C. T.
title: Lipidic α-synuclein fibrils catalyze the formation of pathological mature fibrils

abstract: Materials constructed from interlocking and tangled fibers are challenging to model and understand due in part to the complex interplay between fiber shape and contact mechanics. Much of our intuition about contact mechanics comes from the Hertzian description, which is based on interactions between convex bodies. However, fibers often form clasp shapes, which involve saddle-shaped contact surfaces; the ability for two interacting bodies to conform to each other along a saddle surface confounds many existing mechanical contact models. Following an observation that contact surfaces between fibers tend to look like minimal, constant mean-curvature surfaces, we seek to test this hypothesis and provide a direct link to geometric modeling methods. To do this, we leverage the medial axis transformation, which generalizes the notion of a Voronoi tessellation to generating curves and surfaces. Through computational studies on an orthogonal clasp and a simple knit structure, we find that the medial axis transformation provides a reasonable model for contact surfaces between identical curves. We also show that a generalization of the medial axis transformation based on radical Voronoi tessellations can be used to well-approximate contact surfaces between non-identical curves. We apply this ``radical axis transform'' to curves of different radii and demonstrate a trend for surfaces to adopt finite mean curvature. Our results may point the way towards more sophisticated geometric methods for modeling tangles.

title: Medial Model of Elastic Curve Contacts, from Clasps to Knits

abstract: Self-assembly enables complex structures to emerge from simple building blocks through local interaction rules. Are some structures intrinsically easier to design, that is, do they admit more sets of assembly rules than others? And, can this be predicted from their geometry? We address these questions using a three-dimensional polycube model with programmable face-to-face binding, defining a structure's assembly rule probability as the chance that a randomly chosen rule set produces it. For polycubes, this probability decreases exponentially with assembly complexity, the minimum information required to specify a structure's assembly rules. Intuitively, this follows because structures with low assembly complexity are generated not only by minimal rule sets but also by numerous more elaborate ones, and so arise disproportionately often. Symmetry can reduce assembly complexity by allowing the same building blocks and local interactions to be reused across different parts of a structure. Indeed, we find that the highest probability structures come from a tiny subset of highly symmetric structures. However, symmetry alone does not determine assembly complexity. Structures with the same symmetry can differ substantially in the amount of assembly information they require, depending on how effectively their global symmetry can be exploited by local growth rules. Overall, our results link information, symmetry, and assembly rule probability and suggest that identifying which geometric features permit rule reuse is central to designing minimal programmable self-assembling systems.
authors: Prarthana Agrawal, Joakim Bohlin, Ard A. Louis
title: How symmetry and complexity shape three-dimensional programmable self-assembly

abstract: Lipid bilayers are central to cellular organization and function, yet their atomistic modelling remains constrained by its high computational cost. While coarse-grained (CG) models can overcome this bottleneck, they are limited in accuracy due to the use of simplified functional forms based on molecular mechanics. Using a hybrid functional form combining physics-based terms with a graph neural network, we present implicit-solvent, machine-learned CG models for POPC. When trained on single-lipid data, the model recovers the atomistic conformational landscape. By adding short atomistic simulations of a small flat bilayer to the training data and combining force matching with a denoising objective, we train a model that accurately reproduces bilayer structure and dynamics, in closer agreement with the atomistic reference than existing models, like Martini3 and DryMartini. Beyond its training data, the model stabilizes curved geometries, including vesicles, and captures complex cooperative phenomena such as bilayer and vesicle self-assembly and pore sealing. While limitations remain, particularly regarding chemical transferability, our results establish machine-learned coarse-grained potentials as a promising path towards robust and accurate CG models of lipids and membranes.

title: Exploring the World of Lipids with Machine-Learned Coarse-Grained Models

abstract: Hyperuniform fluids suppress density fluctuations at large length scales, but microscopic protocols for designing their asymptotic scaling remain limited. Here we show how effective driving noise generated by particle dynamics can select the hyperuniform exponent while preserving ordinary diffusion and pairwise center-of-mass conservation of the organized particles. We establish this connection through two protocols based on biased random organization (BRO). First, a two-dimensional BRO layer is nonreciprocally coupled to a three-dimensional Brownian gas through density-dependent kick amplitudes. Bulk density fluctuations generate spatially nonlocal noise with a $q^3$ power spectrum in the adiabatic limit, producing $S(q\to0)\sim q^1$. Second, we introduce reciprocal kicks whose lengths follow a Pareto-like distribution, $P(\ell)\sim\ell^{-1-b}$. For $2<b<4$, the finite second moment supports ordinary diffusion, while the divergent fourth moment changes the long-wavelength noise spectrum to $q^b$. The corresponding fluctuating density field theory predicts continuously tunable hyperuniform scaling, $S(q\to0)\sim q^{b-2}$, supported by particle simulations. Together, these results connect targeted hyperuniform scaling to explicit microscopic dynamics and provide a physical basis for designing collective density correlations in nonequilibrium particle systems.
authors: Yusheng Lei, Yuhan Peng, Ran Ni
title: Designing tunable hyperuniformity in random organization through nonlocal noise

abstract: Particle-resolved colloid simulations are often limited by the fastest microscopic time scale retained in the model, which can be many orders of magnitude shorter than the collective process of interest. This is especially restrictive for aggregating colloids, where explicit near-contact potentials force the time integration to resolve the rapid positional relaxation of bonded pairs within narrow attractive wells. Here we introduce an overdamped constraint-based Brownian dynamics method that replaces the time-resolved integration of stiff near-contact forces by a geometric projection step. After each free Brownian update, hard-sphere exclusion, sticky bonds, and hard-wall interactions are enforced by projecting the particle positions onto the constrained configuration set. The method preserves hard-sphere structure and diffusion, recovers the aggregation kinetics of sticky hard spheres, and extends the physical time reached at fixed computational cost by one to two orders of magnitude relative to the explicit-potential simulations tested here. This acceleration makes Brownian-dominated, low-Péclet electrophoretic deposition accessible to particle-scale simulations, revealing a pathway in which the suspension first densifies and only subsequently develops a bonded network. Implemented as a LAMMPS fix, the framework provides a modular route to long-time Brownian simulations of dense constrained colloidal systems.

title: Long-time Brownian dynamics of hard and sticky colloids by geometric projection

abstract: Boundary conditions strongly influence bacterial turbulence, motivating the question of how hydrated porous substrates affect near-interface collective motion. We characterize the spatiotemporal dynamics of dilute and dense Escherichia coli suspensions above agar substrates of varying concentrations, with glass serving as a nonporous reference. In dense suspensions shortly after loading, collective in-plane kinetic energy varies nonmonotonically with agar concentration, while individual swimming energy and characteristic spatial scales show comparatively little variation. Over five minutes above agar, the collective flow attenuates strongly, accompanied by shorter spatial correlations, longer temporal correlations, and a greater relative spectral weight at higher wavenumbers. To explore how the porous boundary may contribute to these changes, we extend mean-field kinetic theory (MFKT) to incorporate normal seepage and tangential slip at the interface. Linear stability analysis distinguishes near-interface collective modes from those in the bulk and identifies how fluid-layer thickness and permeability-dependent slip length modify the instability cutoff. The predicted reduction in the associated length scale provides a qualitative interpretation of the smaller flow structures observed over time and at higher agar concentrations. These findings reveal distinct substrate-dependent changes in the intensity, persistence, and spatial organization of near-interface bacterial turbulence.
authors: Zixiang Lin, Jin Zhu, Hongyi Bian, Zijie Qu
title: Hydrated porous substrates modulate the spatiotemporal dynamics of bacterial turbulence

abstract: Human movements remain accurate across substantial variations in mechanical loading, yet how the nervous system anticipates and compensates for intrinsic and extrinsic forces when generating muscle commands remains unresolved. Because the forces acting on the body are complex and nonlinear, dynamical modeling provides a powerful framework for identifying the computations underlying motor control. Here, we exploited parabolic flight to dissociate gravitational loading from intrinsic limb dynamics and directly test how these mechanical components are represented in motor commands. We analyzed kinematics and shoulder muscle activity from nine participants performing visually guided pointing movements in microgravity (0g), normogravity (1g), and hypergravity (2g). Inverse dynamics revealed that the gravity-independent component of muscle torque remained invariant across gravitational conditions. In striking contrast, muscle moments estimated from muscle activation showed systematic scaling of not only static but also phasic components with gravitational load, particularly during movement deceleration. This divergence arises because activation-derived muscle moments capture cocontraction, and thus impedance-related control, that is absent from net torques obtained by inverse dynamics. Gravity-dependent regression analyses further showed that muscle activation could be reconstructed from a compact set of mechanical variables dominated by gravity-dependent torque and movement velocity, revealing a low-dimensional structure of motor control. Together, these findings support a control architecture in which motor commands integrate predictive compensation for limb dynamics with gravity-dependent regulation of muscle cocontraction. This dual strategy provides a mechanism for maintaining stable and accurate movement across changing mechanical environments and offers a unified framework for understanding motor control under variable external loads.

abstract: Single-particle cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM), a powerful class of techniques in structural biology with the potential to resolve molecular ensembles, requires that samples be vitrified to protect them from the high vacuum of the electron microscope. However, the effects of vitrification on biomolecular ensembles are unknown. To study them, we carried out extensive molecular dynamics simulations (over 50 ms) of the Trp-cage miniprotein at equilibrium and undergoing rapid cooling. We simulated seven cooling rates spanning three orders of magnitude, with the slowest coolings matching experimental rates. By inspecting molecular mobility and density-temperature trajectories for water with and without protein, we found that water vitrification is unaltered by the protein. To track protein conformation changes, and to relate them to kinetics, we made a Markov State Model (MSM) of Trp-cage from 5.4 ms of equilibrium sampling at 277 K. We observed that MSM states with a characteristic time longer than the duration of the nonequilibrium cooling tend to be more robust to artifacts induced by such cooling. Critically, although we observe that some states vanish in the equilibrium ensemble at 230 K, none do in our nonequilibrium cooled ensembles. To account for these perturbations, we developed a thermodynamic inference framework for recovering equilibrium populations from vitrified ensembles. These results indicate that cryo-EM has the capacity to be an accurate technique for the study of biomolecular ensembles.
authors: Robert Clark, Louis G. Smith, Matthew P. Leighton, Ryan J. Szukalo, Syma Khalid, Pablo G. Debenedetti, Pilar Cossio, Miro A. Astore, Sonya M. Hanson
title: Cooling fast and slow: Characterizing the effects of vitrification in cryo-EM and the subsequent recovery of equilibrium populations

abstract: Mechanical disturbances such as seismic shaking can set a granular slope in motion. Understanding the resulting transport before arrest is important for predicting topographic change, assessing landslide hazards and controlling powder flows in industrial processes. Experiments show that smaller disturbances can trigger avalanches and larger areas are mobilized as slopes approach their stability limit. Yet how much transport varies between events under the same macroscopic conditions and forcing remains unclear. Here we use numerical simulations to show that transport variability is amplified near the critical angle. We apply identical basal pulses to static granular layers with the same macroscopic conditions but different initial particle configurations. Although the mean transport increases approximately in inverse proportion to the angular distance from the critical angle, the standard deviation increases even faster and can exceed the mean. Thus, identical forcing can produce widely different transport amounts. Deterministic constitutive laws that assign a unique response to given macroscopic conditions cannot capture this variability. We introduce fluctuations into the energy balance to develop a stochastic model that captures the main features of the broadening transport distribution. These results show that assessing transport near the critical angle requires considering its distribution, not just its mean, and motivate constitutive descriptions that incorporate fluctuations.
authors: Fumiaki Nakai, Yuto Sasaki
title: Amplified transport variability in granular slope flows near the critical angle

abstract: Topological defects are commonly characterized by their charge, although defects with the same charge can have different internal morphologies. We study the annihilation of isolated $\pm1$ defect pairs in a two-dimensional compressible Toner--Tu model, varying the morphology of the $+1$ defect while keeping the initial charges and separation fixed. Activity produces a morphology-dependent mobility asymmetry: reversing the radial orientation of an aster reverses which defect travels farther, and asters show the strongest response. An early-time analysis reveals that the initial morphology selects distinct density modes whose gradients subsequently feed back on the polarization. Consistently, removing the density-gradient coupling strongly suppresses the asymmetry. These results establish defect morphology, in addition to topological charge, as a dynamical variable governing defect-pair motion in active polar matter.
authors: Abhra Puitandy, Shradha Mishra
title: Topology Does Not Determine Defect Mobility in Active Polar Matter

abstract: Understanding how nonequilibrium systems evolve between distinct statistical regimes remains a fundamental challenge in statistical physics. Here we show that particle deposition at an evaporating contact line provides an experimental realization of cooperative one-dimensional deposition, in which post-deposition capillary attraction drives particles to migrate, cluster, and coarsen. As deposition proceeds, the cluster-width distribution undergoes a striking re-entrant transition, evolving from an initial exponential form to a peaked Gamma distribution and subsequently returning to an exponential form. This dynamic transition is accompanied by a non-monotonic crossover in fluctuation scaling, $σ_w\sim\langle w\rangle^κ$, with $κ$ changing successively from $1$ to $1/2$ and back to $1$. Monte Carlo simulations reproduce these statistical transitions. Our results establish evaporative contact-line deposition as a simple model of correlated one-dimensional assembly and reveal how local interactions can produce re-entrant statistical behaviour in a nonequilibrium system.
authors: Arundas Chandradasan, Dileep Mampallil
title: Capillary Coarsening Drives Re-entrant Statistical Transitions in Early Coffee-Ring Growth

abstract: Adrenal gland-induced hypertension results from underlying adrenal gland disorders including Conn's syndrome, Cushing's syndrome, and Pheochromocytoma. Due to the limitations of existing pharmaceutical and surgical treatment methods, minimally invasive treatment options like microwave ablation (MWA) have received significant attention for treating adrenal gland disorders. A precise comprehension of the dielectric properties of human adrenal glands will help to tailor energy delivery for MWA therapy, thus offering the potential to optimise treatments and minimise damage to surrounding tissues. This study reports the ex vivo dielectric properties of human adrenal glands, including the cortex, medulla, capsule, and tumours, based on the data obtained from four patients (diagnosed with Conn's syndrome, Cushing's syndrome, and Pheochromocytoma) who underwent unilateral adrenalectomy at the University Hospital Galway, Ireland. An open-ended coaxial probe measurement technique was used to measure the dielectric properties for a frequency range of 0.5-8.5 GHz. The dielectric properties were fitted using a two-pole Debye model, and a weighted least squares method was employed to optimise the model parameters. Moreover, the dielectric properties of adrenal tissues and tumours were compared across frequencies commonly used in MWA, including 915 MHz, 2.45 GHz, and 5.8 GHz. The study found that the dielectric properties of adrenal tumours were influenced by the presence of lipid-rich adenomas, and the dielectric properties of Cushing's syndrome tumour were lowest in comparison to the tumours in patients diagnosed with Conn's syndrome and Pheochromocytoma. Furthermore, a notable difference was observed in the dielectric properties of the medulla and cortex among patients diagnosed with Conn's syndrome, Cushing's syndrome, and Pheochromocytoma.

title: Dielectric characterisation of human adrenal glands and adrenal tumours for the development of microwave ablation technologies for hypertension treatment

abstract: The dielectric properties of biological tissues are used to investigate the interaction of electromagnetic (EM) fields with the human body. These properties are integrated into EM numerical simulations, such as the finite difference time domain (FDTD) method, using dielectric models such as Cole-Cole and Debye models. These computational tools are employed to study the propagation of EM waves within the human body. This paper has developed the one-pole and two-pole Cole-Cole and Debye models for the dielectric properties of normal and diseased human trabecular bone tissue at microwave frequencies (0.5-8.5 GHz). The dielectric properties of normal trabecular and cortical bone were derived based on the literature, while those of diseased human trabecular bones (osteoporotic and osteoarthritis) were acquired from a previous study conducted by the authors, which characterised the properties within the 0.5-8.5 GHz frequency range. This study has employed a weighted least squares method to optimise the one-pole and two-pole dielectric models' parameters. The accuracy of the developed dielectric models is validated by comparing the simulated results with the experimental data already published by the authors. The comparative analysis of the models demonstrated that the one-pole Cole-Cole model achieved a better fit compared to the one-pole Debye model across all bone types. Additionally, the two-pole Cole-Cole model exhibited a better fit than the two-pole Debye model. The proposed models can be used in numerical simulations to investigate the interaction of EM fields with bone tissue and develop and optimise microwave bone health monitoring and treatment techniques.
authors: Bilal Amin, Amra Mehboob, Eoghan Dunne, Ana González-Suárez, Finn Krewer, Aoife Lowery, Martin O'Halloran, Adnan Elahi
title: Dielectric Models of Normal and Diseased Human Trabecular Bones at Microwave Frequencies

abstract: Wormlike micellar solutions exhibit formulation-dependent nonlinear startup responses, including stress overshoot, undershoot, and strain hardening, making prediction across compositions and shear rates challenging. We developed a multi-fidelity machine-learning framework to predict stress-growth curves in cetylpyridinium chloride (CPyCl)-based wormlike micelles from sparse experimental measurements. The framework combines a low-fidelity analytical model describing the overall startup response with high-fidelity experimental data capturing formulation-specific nonlinear features. This approach addresses the limited and uneven coverage of salt chemistry, concentration, and shear rate without relying solely on data-intensive neural-network training. The trained model predicts complete stress-growth responses at untested shear rates and enables extraction of strain-hardening characteristics from interpolated curves. By augmenting sparse rheological measurements, the framework provides a basis for exploring relationships among formulation variables, linear viscoelastic properties, and nonlinear startup behavior, while supporting more efficient characterization of wormlike micellar solutions.
authors: Saghar Zolfaghari, Nunzia Lauriello, Ilaria Cusano, Marcello Ferranti, Rossana Pasquino, Safa Jamali
title: Multi-Fidelity Machine Learning for Predicting Startup Stress Growth and Strain Hardening in Wormlike Micellar Solutions

abstract: The method of regularized Stokeslets (MRS) is widely used to model fluid-structure interactions of microscopic bodies in viscous environments. Specifically, MRS computes the fluid velocity generated by regularized forces distributed on an immersed body, which in turn defines a system of ordinary differential equations with which to evolve the body so that the no-slip condition is enforced. To accurately model material properties such as elasticity and bending rigidity, the resulting ODE system is often stiff and, therefore, computationally expensive to solve with explicit time-integration methods. Here we demonstrate the potential of linearly implicit Rosenbrock (ROS) time integration methods to greatly reduce the computational time required to solve such ODE systems. We focus on the classic model problem of the swimming of a flexible filament driven by preferred curvature forcing. Our findings indicate that, compared to previous MRS simulations, the increased stability of ROS methods allows for speed-ups between twenty and two thousand times over explicit Runge-Kutta (ERK) methods. Moreover, we present approximate scaling laws for this speedup as a function of the key model parameters (bending rigidity and slenderness) at the root of numerical stiffness. Lastly, beyond the basic ROS approach, we discuss several additional strategies that further improve performance.
authors: Moslem Uddin, Lisa J. Fauci, Ricardo Cortez, Tommaso Buvoli
title: Improving the performance of regularized Stokeslet simulations using Rosenbrock time integration methods

abstract: Microtubule architecture and dynamics are modulated by small molecules, but how these compounds alter lattice properties and interactions with cellular regulators remains incompletely understood. We used the neuronal microtubule-associated protein doublecortin (DCX), previously reported to preferentially recognize 13-protofilament microtubules, to probe lattices stabilized by different taxanes, including the fluorescent taxane Fchitax-3. We show that DCX binds 15-protofilament Fchitax-3-stabilized microtubules, demonstrating that DCX is not a specific marker of 13-protofilament architecture. Cryo-electron microscopy revealed that the fluorescent moiety of Fchitax-3 inserts into inter-protofilament lateral contacts, explaining its effects on microtubule architecture and dynamics. DCX binds Fchitax-3 microtubules through its N-terminal DC domain, which accommodates the narrower inter-protofilament binding site in the 15-protofilament lattice. Remarkably, although Fchitax-3 induces the longitudinal lattice expansion characteristic of taxanes, DCX remodels its binding site towards its preferred compacted configuration. Thus, taxanes can modify microtubule structure in distinct ways while preserving lattice plasticity and the capacity to undergo conformational remodelling by microtubule-associated proteins. This contrasts with the comparatively rigid lattice of GMPCPP-stabilized microtubules. Consequently, interpretations of microtubule lattice states based on comparisons between taxane- and GMPCPP-stabilized microtubules may conflate structural differences with different degrees of lattice plasticity. Our findings establish the microtubule lattice as a malleable structural substrate whose drug-induced conformations can be further remodelled by cellular binding partners.
authors: Ramaswamy, V.; Manka, S. W.; Sharma, D. D.; Akhmanova, A.; Rai, A.; Moores, C.
title: STRUCTURAL PLASTICITY ALLOWS DOUBLECORTIN AND DRUG-STABILIZED MICROTUBULES TO ACCOMMODATE EACH OTHER

abstract: We demonstrate that the enzymatic activity of alpha-amylase (AA) can serve as an effective physicochemical trigger for membrane remodeling in giant unilamellar vesicles (GUVs). This work provides insight into how primitive protocellular reactions directly translate into the membrane's mechanical responses. Analysis of the potato starch utilized in this work is composed of ~26\% amylose and ~75\% amylopectin. Quantitative DNS analysis revealed time- and concentration-dependent accumulation of reducing sugars during starch degradation by AA. The HPLC-RID chromatograms demonstrated the synthesis of glucose, maltose, maltotriose, maltotetraose, maltopentaose, maltohexaose, and maltoheptaose, with maltose and maltotriose as the major products. The accumulation of these soluble hydrolysis products gradually increases the osmolarity of the extracellular medium surrounding the vesicles, leading to osmotic asymmetry across the membrane. This biochemical framework provides a quantitative basis for understanding membrane deformation, curvature generation, vesicle deflation, and budding. In addition to the specific starch--$\alpha$-amylase system studied here, our work uncovers a general mechanism by which external biochemical reactions control membrane shape transformations via osmotic coupling. Such enzyme-driven remodeling offers a simple yet powerful strategy for inducing dynamic structural changes in artificial cells. It may provide insight into primitive protocellular processes in which metabolic activity and membrane mechanics were inherently coupled.

title: A Saliva-Inspired Model of Enzymatic Starch Hydrolysis by Alpha Amylase

abstract: Quasi-periodic pressure pulses associated with cardiac and respiratory activity generate reciprocating cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) motion in the human ventricles. Regular waves dominated by the cardiac cycle are overlaid with cycles of low-frequency respiratory waves, the latter to become stronger in forced breathing or even dominated by large successive flushes in NREM sleep. The present study investigates how such waves contribute to residual streaming within the human ventricles. Transient CFD simulations were performed in the third ventricle at varying parameters of frequency, stroke volume and wave-form asymmetry. Increasing the aqueduct peak Reynolds-number, either by small stroke volume and high frequency or large stroke volume at low frequency, transfers the flow from a reversible flow pattern to the formation of clear preferential pathways, alternating between the in- and outflow cycle. The resulting permanent streaming flux across the aqueduct relative to the mean oscillatory flow-rate, i.e. the dimensionless streaming ratio SR follows a rational saturation relation, SR [~] ReAq,peak/(C + ReAq,peak), demonstrating that increasing the peak aqueduct Reynolds number yields diminishing returns and bounds the relative contribution of residual inter-ventricular streaming. These findings demonstrate differences in hydrodynamic organisation in the third ventricle and highlight the importance of this organisation for intraventricular fluid exchange.
authors: Zhao, P.; McTavish, L.; Bruecker, C.
title: Organised streaming of cerebrospinal fluid in the human third ventricle

abstract: Soft cancer cells embedded in stiffer epithelial layers migrate in bursts, which prior simulations have attributed to their deformability. In a dense layer, however, interfacial tension sets two things at once: the energy cost of a deformation and the rate at which it relaxes. Here we disentangle the two in an active phase-field model of a near-confluent monolayer in which relaxation rate and free energy can be varied independently. Crowding slows cells not by pushing them back bodily but through the relaxation of their own deformations against neighbours, which cancels most of their propulsion. Slowing this relaxation in a minority of cells, at unchanged energetics and propulsion, more than doubles their transport and speeds up the untouched majority by half. Conversely, the advantage of soft cells vanishes, and at high soft-cell fractions reverses, once their relaxation is made as fast as that of normal cells. Independent of composition, mixtures transport like a uniform layer with the geometric-mean interfacial tension. Passive relaxation kinetics thus emerges as an independent lever on transport, suggesting that the fluidity of heterogeneous tissues may depend on how quickly cells recover their shape, not only on how stiff they are.
authors: Silber, S. A.; Karttunen, M.
title: Relaxation kinetics controls cell transport in crowded active monolayers

abstract: The human Tat-interactive protein, 60 kilodalton (Tip60) histone acetyltransferase (HAT) complex (NuA4/TIP60 complex, from now on TIP60-C) is a central regulator of chromatin accessibility, coupling histone acetylation with transcriptional activation and genome stability. But how the catalytic HAT module engages its nucleosome substrate has remained unknown. Here we present the structure of the human TIP60-C HAT module bound to the nucleosome, revealing a defined binding architecture in which TIP60, EPC1, ING3, and MEAF6 cooperatively position the catalytic center on the nucleosome surface, with the HAT module anchored on the histone acidic patch and engaging the linker DNA. The structure uncovers an intramolecular interaction involving the N-terminal Tudor domain of the TIP60 acetyltransferase subunit that suggests a potential mechanism for autoregulation of HAT activity. Together, our findings define the core principles by which the human TIP60-C HAT module recognizes chromatin, establishing a structural foundation for understanding how TIP60-C modifies chromatin in metazoans.
authors: Yang, Z.; Florez Ariza, A. J.; Cote, J.; Nogales, E.
title: Structural basis of nucleosome recognition by the human NuA4/TIP60 acetyltransferase complex

abstract: The protein -synuclein (-syn) plays a central role in several neurodegenerative diseases, including Parkinson's disease; however, its physiological function remains enigmatic. We provide direct evidence by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, microscale thermophoresis (MST), and biolayer interferometry (BLI) measurements that the -synuclein C-terminus binds to the vesicular SNARE (soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptor) protein synaptobrevin-2 (syb-2), also known as VAMP2 (vesicle-associated membrane protein). The observed dissociation constant (Kd) in the 10 - 50 micromolar range falls within the estimated concentration range of -synuclein in neurons, while local concentrations may be substantially higher. NMR chemical shift perturbation (CSP) and paramagnetic relaxation enhancement (PRE) experiments mapped the binding site with residue-specific resolution to the -synuclein C-terminus (V118 - E137) and to the synaptobrevin-2 SNARE motif/linker domain interface (region A82 - K87), and also affected the synaptobrevin-2 N-terminus (M1 - S2). NMR CSPs and PREs indicate a transient interaction in the fast exchange (s-ms) regime. These transient weak binding interactions are characteristic of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and allow both proteins to engage in multiple binding interactions, thereby enabling -synuclein to play a regulatory role upstream of or during neuronal exocytosis. While the exact physiological role of -synuclein remains debated, the involvement of its pathological form in several neurodegenerative diseases (dubbed synucleinopathies) is well established. Our data suggest a direct link between proteins involved in neurodegeneration and neuronal exocytosis.
authors: Werner, S.; Stief, T.; Schulz, C. M.; Vormann, K.; Backer, R.; Schutzmann, M. P.; Gremer, L.; Hoyer, W.; Lakomek, N.-A.
title: Direct NMR evidence for transient binding of the vesicular SNARE protein synaptobrevin-2/VAMP2 to the α-synuclein C-terminus

abstract: Microtubule-condensate interactions regulate cytoskeletal dynamics involved in cell division, vesicle transport and cellular locomotion. Due to the size of microtubules and the slow timescale of condensate structural relaxation, there has not been a systematic investigation at the molecular level as to what binding patterns (molecular grammar) enable condensate binding to microtubules. We provide a simulation protocol that is able to predict whether any given disordered protein sequence will bind to microtubules.

title: Molecular Grammar of Microtubule-Wetting Condensates

abstract: Autonomous microrobots navigating biological vasculature could enable targeted drug delivery and thrombolysis, yet training control policies for physiologically complex environments remains an open challenge. Prior reinforcement learning (RL) studies of microrobotic navigation have largely used idealized geometries lacking realistic flow in confined branching, and dense cellular obstacles. Here, we develop a physically grounded, deliberately idealized two-dimensional capillary simulation, with resolved flow fields, explicit red blood cell dynamics, and schematic-derived branching geometry, training RL agents via an advection-dominated concentration field driven by physiological flow speeds. Mapping success across robot size and swimming speed, we show via zero-shot transfer that most training failures reflect optimization limits, not physical ones. A policy transferred from a more demanding condition succeeds far beyond where per-combination training converges. Its eventual collapse offers a tentative lower bound on what is physically achievable. Successful agents converge on Run-and-Rotate strategies. The transferred policy, a variant of this family, shows a distinctive profile, that we believe is responsible for its exceptional transfer success. Without retraining, these agents perform targeted blocking and unblocking of individual vessel branches, restoring red blood cell passage toward baseline levels and suggesting RL as a viable framework for microrobotic intervention in biological networks.
authors: Drotleff, Jannik, Hohenberger, Paul, Tovey, Samuel, Lohrmann, Christoph, Hoßbach, Julian, Nikolaou, Konstantin, Holm, Christian
title: Reinforcement learning enables autonomous microrobot navigation and intervention in simulated blood capillaries

abstract: Fluorescent dyes conjugated to monoclonal antibodies specifically trastuzumab (TRAS) and pertuzumab (PERT) serve as sensitive reporters of changes in the local energetic environment arising from antibody-antibody and antibody-antigen interactions. Upon covalent conjugation, the antibody local environment perturbates the energetic state of the dye, resulting in changes of the fluorescence emission energy and emission width of the dye. The dependence of these spectral parameters on antibody concentration was measured in HBS-8, diluted and undiluted human serum. In addition, the emission energy and emission width of dye-conjugated TRAS were investigated as a function of recombinant human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) extracellular domain concentration in HBS-8 and in diluted and undiluted human serum. Antibody-antibody and antibody-antigen interactions produce remarkable contributions into the emission energy and emission width. These contributions depend on the composition of the surrounding medium. Our study showed that the samples containing 100 nM TRAS in serum exhibited the largest spectral changes upon interaction with HER2 suggesting that antibody-antigen interaction are not linear across concentration range of the antibodies. Moreover, our results demonstrate that interactions between dye-conjugated antibodies and their binding partners can be detected under physiologically relevant conditions. These findings establish fluorescence emission energy and emission width analysis as a potential approach for probing antibody interactions in complex biological matrices.
authors: Thiyagaraj, D.; Del Re, A.; Pham, Q. D.; Gomez Garrote, I.; Saudi, A.; Fedorych, O.
title: Influence of antibody-antigen interaction on fluorescence of Rhodamine 6G conjugated to the antibodies measured in human serum

abstract: Sarbanes et al. find that loss of tubulin autoregulation mediator TTC5 in both human and mouse cortical neurons drives altered neuronal morphology and increased motility and connect this to reduced tubulin availability and microtubule dynamics. These findings provide an underlying basis for neurodevelopmental pathology seen in patients with TTC5 mutations.

abstract: Capillary networks are classically viewed as passive conduits that supply energy to active neural tissue. Whether microvascular organization can also contribute to functional communication between adjacent brain regions remains largely unexplored. The nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS) and area postrema (AP) form a brainstem complex that coordinates homeostatic regulation; however, the organization and functional significance of their shared microcirculation remain unknown. Previous anatomical studies identified direct capillary connections between the NTS and AP, demonstrating a continuous microvascular network between two anatomically distinct regions. Here, we used in vivo two-photon microscopy, combined with fluorescent vascular labeling and analysis of red blood cell dynamics, to investigate the blood flow within the shared NTS-AP microvasculature. Blood flow across these junctions is predominantly unidirectional, flowing from the NTS towards AP. Morphometric analyses reveal that AP capillaries are significantly larger than those in the NTS, providing a structural basis for this flow asymmetry. Despite these geometric differences, capillary flow velocities are preserved across regions, indicating active regulation of perfusion within the shared network. These findings reveal directional blood flow within a shared AP-NTS capillary network, identifying a potential vascular route by which diffusible signals generated in one region may preferentially reach the other.
authors: Carson, Kaitlin E., Roy, Ranjan, Stern, Javier E.
title: Directional blood flow within a shared capillary network links the nucleus of the solitary tract and area postrema in rats

abstract: Cells maintain asymmetric electrochemical environments across selectively permeable plasma membranes. Ion channels on plasma membranes redistribute small ions, whereas large openings such as gasdermin pores allow both ions and proteins to cross the membrane, generating a multispecies transport regime. The transport of charged ions and proteins shapes electrochemical environments, leading to osmolarity changes, which in turn promotes water influx and cell swelling. Although biologists have observed the phenotypic progression from pore formation to cell swelling for decades, the molecular transport events underlying this progression remain elusive. To elucidate how pore formation drives downstream cellular effects, we establish quantitative multispecies transport frameworks to investigate gasdermin-perforated cells. We start by developing a reductionist model and benchmarking it against analytical Donnan predictions. We then explore three-dimensional geometries containing individual pores or pore clusters that form either simultaneously or sequentially. We reveal that ion-protein timescale separation generates non-canonical Donnan-like states, pore and cargo properties tune local transport, pore clustering modulates osmotic gradients, and sequential pore formation produces feedback-dependent dynamics. This work deepens our mechanistic understanding of cellular responses to membrane damage and informs the therapeutic design of pore-forming proteins with tunable cellular effects.
authors: Guan, Y.; Li, H.; Shi, M.; Sajbel, K.; Gao, Y. B.; Xia, S.
title: Multispecies transport shapes electrochemical environments in perforated cells

abstract: Living systems operate far from thermodynamic equilibrium, sustaining complexity through continuous free-energy influx and heat dissipation. Yet the higher-order functional constraints imposed by non-equilibrium dynamics remain largely unexplored. To formalize how changes in cellular entropy production constrain intracellular organization across proliferative state transitions, we developed a stochastic-thermodynamic model linking reduced dissipative drive to transient increases in intracellular configurational entropy. Within this framework, we examined abundance-weighted predicted RNA folding stability as a transcriptome-level projection of the intracellular configurational remodelling. Consistent with the model, transcriptome reorganization across the cell cycle produces coordinated, phase-dependent changes in the distribution of transcript-level RNA folding free energies. Extending this analysis to stress adaptation, we find that human cancer cells exposed to molecularly targeted agents and nutrient-limited Escherichia coli converge on expressed RNA pools enriched for transcripts with less negative RNA folding free energies, despite marked heterogeneity in the transcriptional responses within each system. Opposing shifts during acquired resistance under continued drug exposure and bacterial recovery from starvation further support an association with growth state. Together, these findings suggest that transcriptome organization extends beyond gene-regulatory programs to collective biophysical properties that may reflect non-equilibrium constraints shaping cellular-state transitions.
authors: Zivieri, R.; Reeves, J.; Pattnaik, S.; Martins Reis, A.; Xu, A.; Thomas, D. M.; Deveson, I. W.; Cipponi, A.
title: A conserved thermodynamic signature links transcriptome organization to growth state

abstract: Xenopus laevis embryos survive teratogenic stress at significantly higher rates in larger groups, a phenomenon termed cross-embryo morphogenetic assistance (CEMA) (Tung, Sperry et al. 2024). We introduce topoiesis, a proposed mechanism by which a constitutively secreted stress signal (extracellular ATP or adenosine) diffuses and decays across the group, accumulating more in larger groups where interior volume outpaces absorbing surface. We find that this rising field carries more embryos to survival and demarcates the collective more sharply from its surroundings as collective screening strength grows with size. At intermediate sizes the outcome is spatially organized (a rescued interior enclosed by a failing periphery) and reconstitutes after shuffling. In larger groups the field restructures: its peak concentration keeps rising while its interior gradient flattens into a near-uniform bulk bounded by a sharp rim, sharpening demarcation while blurring distinctions among interior members. This pre-pattern stabilizes well before individual fate commitment, opening a window in which collective geometry can act on survival outcome. A biophysically calibrated minimal model capturing these principles recapitulates CEMA rescue rates across all six observed group sizes (N=1-306; 0%-92%) and the size-dependent craniofacial defect rate among survivors. It predicts that sealing a group's boundary against loss, rather than changing its size or biochemical regulation, moves mean rescue from 0% to 100% and reorganizes the rescue structure, tracking the predicted field geometry. These results reveal a hidden simplicity behind apparent complexity: diffusion and geometry alone may suffice to make a collective both spatially organized and controllable through macroscale intervention rather than microscale engineering of its members.
authors: Manicka, S.; Levin, M.
title: A topoietic model of collective morphogenesis and compartmentalization

abstract: This work presents a Gaussian Boson Sampling (GBS) method to identify densely connected subgraphs from omics-derived gene networks. The method utilises the intrinsic sampling bias of GBS towards densely connected nodes, providing an efficient strategy for sampling dense subgraphs compared with classical methods. We applied GBS to sheep rumen gene pathway networks under low and high methane yield conditions. The networks were naturally grouped into high, moderate, and low abundance clusters without specifying the number of genes per cluster. These clusters were associated with biochemical functions of facultative anaerobes, which may support methanogenic activity by maintaining reducing conditions favourable for methanogens. Benchmarking against the classical Greedy Peel algorithm showed that GBS consistently identified identical densest subgraphs while requiring 5 to 10 times fewer subgraph evaluations. Moreover, GBS obtained more subgraphs with higher densities than uniform random sampling. These results showed that GBS can substantially reduce the number of subgraph evaluations required to identify biologically meaningful gene clusters. However, the present study was conducted using a classical simulator, and investigations using photonic hardware are needed to evaluate the full potential of GBS. Nevertheless, these findings support the future use of GBS for subgraph search in large multi-omic networks where dense modules exhibit functional significance.
authors: Ho, Kin Tung Michael, Lai, Ching-Jui, Tan, Giin Yu Amy, Lee, Po-Heng
title: Gaussian Boson Sampling for efficient dense subgraph identification in omic-driven gene networks during anthropogenic methane emission

abstract: Prolines in the transmembrane (TM) region play a pivotal role in the function of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs). In this molecular simulation study, 2 independent sets of trajectories are analyzed for 7 mutations of TM prolines of β2-adrenergic receptor in agonist (Ag)- and inverse-agonist (IAg)-bound states and compared with the wild-type (WT) receptor. A set of structural and contact-based signatures that consistently separate activating from inactivating mutations is identified. While mutation does not substantially alter local protein structure, it leads to numerous structural changes in the protein that affect activity, largely consistent with results of earlier experiments.

title: Conserved proline mutations preserve helical kinks but rewire the activation networks of β2-adrenergic receptor

abstract: Single-particle imaging with X-ray free-electron lasers can, in principle, be used to study macromolecules with high spatial and temporal resolution, in a near-native state. A significant challenge, however, is the substantial background scattering from the solvent and reduced contrast when imaging proteins in solution. This study investigates the feasibility of overcoming this limitation by leveraging two recent technological breakthroughs: the generation of stable, ultra-thin liquid sheets and the availability of intense, nanometer-sized X-ray beams. Through simulations using the 15 nm GroEL protein complex as a model system, we demonstrate that a structure can be obtained despite the reduced contrast and the presence of a significant water-induced background. While experimental realization will be challenged by radiation damage and positional jitter, our idealized model isolates the fundamental challenge of contrast reduction. We demonstrate that the substantial water background does not inherently prevent algorithms from successfully orienting faint diffraction patterns, allowing the subsequent phase retrieval pipeline to resolve structures.
authors: You, Tong, Maia, Filipe R. N. C.
title: Pattern orientation despite water-induced contrast reduction: a theoretical baseline for ultrafast single-particle X-ray imaging

abstract: Biomolecular condensates form through weak, multivalent, non-covalent interactions, but the role of covalent crosslinks in shaping their assembly and material properties remains poorly understood. We previously showed that disulfide bonds between cysteines in designer phase-separating peptides (PSPs) act as redox-reversible crosslinks that lower the saturation concentration (Csat) and help maintain condensate fluidity. Here, we ask which sequence features govern this behavior. We built two peptide libraries: one varying the inter-cysteine spacer length (2-10 residues) and one varying cysteine density (0-33%). Inter-cysteine spacers tuned condensate properties only modestly. Longer inter-cysteine lengths raised Csat from 300 to 900 M, showed greater fluidity (as assessed by fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) recovery rate, and resisted loss of fluidity during maturation; all inter-cysteine length variants dissolved and reformed reversibly over three redox cycles. Cysteine density, in contrast, was the dominant control parameter. Increasing cysteine density lowered Csat about 60-fold (1.5 mM to 25 M) and reduced the fluidity by an order of magnitude. Its effect on fluidity was non-monotonic: condensates with up to ~14% cysteine density stayed liquid-like for 10 days, whereas those with 21-33% cysteine density in the peptide showed slower coalescence. Condensates with the highest densities also resisted dissolution under reducing conditions and showed sharply reduced uptake of a protein cargo (eGFP; ~60% to ~9%) and a small molecule (TMR, ~70% to ~45%), consistent with smaller mesh size. Together, these results identify disulfide crosslink density as a key lever for programming condensate assembly, viscoelasticity, redox responsiveness, and porosity. The results offer key design principles both for understanding cysteine-rich disordered proteins in biomolecular condensates and for engineering redox-responsive biomaterials.
authors: Mondal, M.; Swetman, W. S.; Allen, C. T.; Livingston, H.; Clemons, T. D.; Rangachari, V.
title: Disulfide Crosslink Density is a Key Determinant in the Formation, Dynamics, and Maturation of Cysteine-rich Designer Biomolecular Condensates.

abstract: Classic nanofluidic devices harness geometric confinement to modulate single polymer conformation and control chain dynamics. While classic nanofluidic devices have given rise to a range of applications, they are fundamentally limited by the static nature of their construction, which restricts real time control over molecular conformations. The reversible electrokinetic confinement (RECON) technique enables time-dependent control of DNA conformations in nanowells via dynamic modulation of field-induced confinement. Here, we demonstrate that applying dynamically varying confinement using stochastic and periodic signals can drive the confined polymer to access a range of non-equilibrium states, with the distinct configurations quantified via their radius of gyration tensor. For periodic driving, the device allows controlled cycling across conformational states, with distinct hysteresis observed in the shape anisotropy modulation. We quantify the interplay between the driving frequency, driving amplitude, and resulting hysteresis. Overall, our results establish RECON as a platform for active manipulation of single molecules, opening new avenues for studying non-equilibrium polymer physics and developing high-throughput, dynamically tunable nanofluidic devices.
authors: Pessoa, M. A. S.; Reisner, W.
title: Non-equilibrium cyclic conformations of DNA under electrokinetic confinement

abstract: Cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) is emerging as a tool for large-scale ligand screening and fragment-based drug discovery, generating extensive collections of reconstructions. At the same time, the systematic inspection of local density variations remains challenging, particularly when identifying weak or partially occupied features. Here, we present Astex-Faro, a statistical framework that defines an expected specimen state from a reference ensemble and identifies significant structural deviations in a target map through comparison against this reference. Furthermore, the method allows the enhancement of weak or poorly resolved features, enabling the recovery of signals that would otherwise be difficult to interpret. Fourier Shell Coherence (FSCoh) is introduced as a metric that quantifies consistency across reconstruction ensembles. We show that Astex-Faro reliably detects subtle structural features and improves their interpretability across datasets spanning a broad range of experimental challenges, from highly homogeneous specimens to membrane proteins, low-occupancy ligands and fragment-screening experiments. Together, these developments provide a practical framework for cryo-EM screening, increasing confidence in hit identification and reducing the risk of missed binding events.
authors: de Isidro-Gomez, F. P.; Sorzano, C. O. S.; Carazo, J.-M.; Saur, M.
title: Facilitating the identification of cryo-EM hit matter in drug discovery with Astex-Faro

abstract: DNA synapsis is a crucial step in Non-Homologous End Joining. Through molecular-level quantification of the underlying interactions, this work reveals a regulatory mechanism for how APLF-mediated DNA synapsis is restricted to Ku when it is bound to damaged DNA.

title: DNA-driven dimerization of Ku70/Ku80 regulates the synapsis of double-strand breaks by APLF

abstract: Cold numbs our fingers, an effect attributed to cooling effects on skin receptors. Ramirez et al. show that a cold illusion also desensitizes touch, even on a finger that is not physically cooled. A computational model indicates that subjective cold acts on perceptual decision-making, alongside the physical effects of cooling.
authors: Juan Carlos Ramirez, Jose Vergara, Brandon Kim, Hannes P. Saal, Jeffrey M. Yau
title: Illusory cold desensitizes touch

abstract: A precise analysis of shape instabilities in cell-sized membrane compartments requires thorough quantification of the shape dynamics of individual components over extended periods. Herein, we have used phase-contrast microscopy to image giant unilamellar membrane vesicles (GUVs), which are widely used as model systems for cellular structures. GUVs were prepared in the fluid lamellar phase of 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine with and without cholesterol dissolved within a potato starch solution. The morphological changes and budding dynamics of individual GUVs with different chemical compositions were quantified using a deep-learning based image analysis framework over extended time periods, by using phase-contrast micrographs as input data. This automated framework integrates contour-based detection of the mother vesicle with precise segmentation of daughter compartments, thereby enabling explicit identification and tracking of mother and daughter vesicles at high temporal resolution. These findings further facilitate the measurement of the temporal evolution of vesicle morphometrics including area, and local membrane curvature during budding, that can be used as an input to develop computational models aimed at elucidating curvature-driven membrane remodeling in complex soft materials.
authors: Pandey, T.; Kudawla, R.; Negi, S.; Varshan, J. B. S.; Devarakonda, C.; Singh, D.; Chatterjee, A.; Bhatia, T.
title: Evolution of Vesicle Shape Parameters Based on A Deep-Learning Based Image Analysis Framework Over Extended Time Periods

abstract: Repair (sealing) of traumatic plasmalemmal lesions involves the formation, movement, and accumulation of vesicles at the injury site by active transport and by passive bulk flow of cytoplasm. We show that hypotonic and hypertonic salines affect the direction and rate of vesicle movement in severed crayfish medial giant axons (CMGAs), presumably because osmotically-driven changes in intracellular pressure alter bulk cytoplasmic flow along the axon and at the lesion site. We develop a general Hagen-Poiseuille pressure-cable biophysical model of bulk cytoplasmic flow to predict direction and relative rate of cytoplasmic influx and efflux for CMGAs and other axons modeled as fluid-filled cylinders with distributed osmotic water permeability.
authors: Marshal L. Mencel, George D. Bittner
title: Hagen-Poiseuille distributed-pressure model of osmotically-driven cytoplasmic flow in severed axons

abstract: Complex I is a large membrane protein that transduces redox energy into a proton motive force across a biological membrane, powering cellular respiration. Yet, despite significant experimental and computational efforts, its long-range proton translocation mechanism remains poorly understood. Here, we combine nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy and site-directed mutagenesis experiments with multiscale classical and hybrid quantum/classical (QM/MM) simulations to probe how conformational dynamics is linked to proton transfer reactions in the terminal antiporter module (Nqo12/NuoL/ND5) of Complex I. We show that protonation of a conserved proton-loading site (Lys329/His241Nqo12) in the terminal antiporter-like module gives rise to conformational changes that result in opening of the proton pathway. We further show that this protonation reaction is controlled by buried ion-pairs that modulate the barrier for proton translocation by intrinsic electric field effects. On a general level, our combined findings reveal how bioenergetic machines combine conformational dynamics with hydration transitions to establish efficient redox-driven proton pumps.
authors: Liebau, J.; Saura, P.; Badolato, S.; Gamiz-Hernandez, A. P.; Kaila, V. R. I.
title: Electrostatic control of conformational dynamics drives proton translocation in respiratory Complex I

abstract: Using an impinging flow device, we investigate how spatial shear stress gradients shape microvascular endothelial cell mechanics and collective migration. In response to flow endothelial cells slow down and migrate against the flow, while enhancing their traction and monolayer stresses through distinct FAK- and TGF-β1-dependent mechanisms.
